name: Kolmogorov Complexity
statement: The complexity of an object is the length of the shortest program that produces it.
statementAccent: the shortest program that produces it
meaning: The Kolmogorov complexity of a string is the length of the shortest computer program, in a fixed universal language, that outputs that string and halts. It measures the object's information content: an object is simple if it has a short description and complex, or random, if its shortest description is essentially itself.
mechanism: Fix a universal machine, and the complexity of a string is the size of the smallest program that makes the machine print it. The choice of machine matters only up to a constant: the invariance theorem says that for any two universal languages, the complexities of a string differ by at most a fixed constant independent of the string. So complexity is machine-independent up to that additive constant, which makes the measure objective and absolute in the limit. Incompressibility is randomness: the less a string can be shortened, the more random it is.

examples.text: The string 'ab' repeated a thousand times has a tiny description — 'write ab a thousand times' — while a string of random characters of the same length has no shorter description than itself, so it is nearly incompressible.

A counting argument shows there are far too few short programs to describe all strings, so the overwhelming majority of strings of a given length cannot be compressed by even a few bits — genuine randomness is the rule, not the exception.
An object's Kolmogorov complexity is the ultimate floor on lossless compression; real compressors like gzip give upper bounds on it but can never in general reach the true minimum.

variants.name: Chaitin's constant
variants.text: The halting probability of a universal machine — the chance a random program halts — which is definable yet algorithmically random and uncomputable, a concrete number embodying the theory's limits.

variants.name: Minimum description length
variants.text: A practical, computable statistical principle inspired by the idea: choose the model that minimises the combined description of the model and the data it explains.

whyItMatters: It gives a rigorous, machine-independent definition of the information content and randomness of an individual object, founding the field of algorithmic information theory. It sharpens what compression, simplicity, and randomness mean, and connects deeply to the limits of proof and computation through Godel and the halting problem.

working.text: gauge an object's regularity by how short a program can generate it — the shorter the description, the more structure it has.
when nothing shorter than the object itself describes it, regard the object as algorithmically random.
since the true complexity is uncomputable, work with the best short description you can find, knowing a shorter one may exist.

limits: Kolmogorov complexity is provably uncomputable: no algorithm can compute it in general, a fact equivalent in strength to solving the halting problem. One can only obtain upper bounds by finding ever-shorter programs, never certify the true minimum. It is also defined only up to an additive constant, so absolute complexity values for specific short objects are not uniquely meaningful — the theory is asymptotic. And it must not be confused with computational complexity, which concerns running time rather than description length.
misreadings: It is not a quantity you can calculate for an arbitrary object — it is uncomputable, and only upper bounds are ever available. And it is not about how long a program takes to run; it is about how short the program can be.
origin: Discovered independently by Ray Solomonoff (1960 and 1964), Andrey Kolmogorov (1965), and Gregory Chaitin (published 1969), each approaching it from inductive inference, randomness, or string structure — a classic case of multiple discovery.

sources.text: Kolmogorov complexity, Wikipedia. — the shortest-program definition, the invariance theorem, uncomputability, and the multiple discovery.
Vitanyi, "An Introduction to Kolmogorov Complexity," CWI. — the discovery history and the invariance property.
